topRepeated.tip: Many common Spanish verbs are irregular in the 'yo' form – memorize these first as they're the most frequent.
'Ser' describes identity and permanent traits; 'estar' describes states, conditions, and locations.
The subjunctive in Spanish expresses subjectivity – wishes, doubts, emotions, and hypotheticals rather than facts.
Spanish questions are framed by '¿' and '?' – the inverted mark at the start helps readers know a question is coming.
The Spanish future tense adds endings to the whole infinitive. Only 12 verbs have irregular stems.
In Spanish, adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they modify: 'casa blanca,' 'coches blancos.'
Formal Spanish uses 'usted/ustedes,' longer sentences, and careful connectors. Informal uses 'tú/vosotros' and contractions.
Spanish idioms rarely translate literally. Learn them as whole phrases – they're essential for natural conversation.
'Querer que' + subjunctive: wanting someone else to do something always requires subjunctive.
Verb periphrases combine two verbs with specific meaning. The first verb conjugates; the second stays infinitive or gerund.

"Che" as relative pronoun: connects a noun to a describing clause. "Il libro che leggo" = The book that I read.

Ouvrir to ouvert: shared pattern with couvrir, découvrir, offrir.

conjugationExamples.tip: Inversion: swap subject and verb and add a hyphen. Vous parlez → Parlez-vous ? This is formal. Add -t- between vowels: A
In inversion with 'il/elle', add -t- between two vowels: 'Parle-t-il ?' The -t- is just for pronunciation.
After negation, 'du/de la/des' become 'de/d'': 'il y a du pain' → 'il n'y a pas de pain'.
'Venir' is an irregular -ir verb: je viens, tu viens, il vient. Note the -ien- stem change.
Background activity (imparfait) + new event (passé composé): 'nous regardions' → then 'il est arrivé'.
Si + imparfait, conditionnel: si nous avions → nous achèterions. Never use conditional after si.
"Devienne" is the subjunctive of devenir. Formed from the ils-form stem: deviennent → devienn-.
For -ir verbs like finir, the subjunctive uses the ils-form stem: finissent → finiss- + subjunctive endings.
Subjunctive of construire: construise. Stem from ils-form: construisent → construis-.
'Ferme' – tu-form imperative of -er verbs drops the -s: 'tu fermes' → 'ferme'. Exception: -er verbs only.

topRepeated.tip: Portuguese comparatives and superlatives usually add 'mais/menos' before the adjective, unlike English which changes the word form.
Many Portuguese verbs change meaning with 'se': reflexive form often shifts focus to the subject experiencing the action.
The pretérito perfeito describes completed, one-time past actions – like the English simple past.
The compound pluperfect (tinha + particípio) is the standard spoken form – the literary simple pluperfect (-ra) is rare in speech.
The imperfect describes ongoing states, habitual actions, or background events in the past – like 'used to' or 'was doing'.
In casual Brazilian Portuguese, the imperative often uses the você form (3rd person singular present).
'Vai + infinitive' forms the informal future for você/ele/ela – 'Ela vai chegar' (She's going to arrive).
Formal Portuguese uses longer connectors and more complex syntax – academic writing avoids contractions like 'pra' and 'pro'.
Portuguese prepositions always contract with definite articles – these fused forms are not optional in standard Portuguese.
The Portuguese preterite marks completed past actions. Regular endings are clear and consistent.

topRepeated.tip: The dative case marks the indirect object (to/for whom). Key dative prepositions: mit, von, zu, bei, nach, aus, seit.
Comparatives add -er (schneller), superlatives use am ...sten (am schnellsten). Many monosyllabic adjectives add umlaut: groß→größer.
Many German verbs are reflexive where English ones aren't: 'sich freuen' (to be happy), 'sich erinnern' (to remember).
In spoken German, Perfekt is the go-to past tense for nearly all verbs – Präteritum is mainly for sein, haben, and modals.
Konjunktiv I signals reported speech in formal contexts – it distances the speaker from the claim: 'Er sagte, er sei müde'.
Adjective endings in German depend on three factors: the article type, the grammatical case, and the noun's gender.
The genitive shows possession: 'das Buch des Lehrers'. It's also required after wegen, trotz, während, statt.
Formal German register uses longer sentences, passive constructions, and Konjunktiv forms – it sounds markedly different from casual speech.
Academic German favors nominal style (using nouns over verbs), complex compounds, and hedging with Konjunktiv II.
Verb chains in German place the conjugated verb second and all other verbs at the end: 'Ich habe ihn kommen sehen'.
The verb goes to the end in subordinate clauses: "...omdat ik werk" (because I work).
Dutch verb stems: remove -en, apply spelling rules (double vowels in closed syllables, devoice z→s, v→f).
"Er" has multiple uses: existential, locative, and prepositional.
Dutch uses V2 word order in main clauses.
Plural subjects (wij/zij/ze) always take the infinitive form: 'wij werken', 'zij lopen'.
'Ik ben' (I am) uses 'zijn' – the most irregular Dutch verb.
In Dutch, 'ik' always takes the bare verb stem – no -t or -en ending.
'Hoe' (how) forms questions about manner or degree: 'Hoe gaat het?'
"Alstublieft" (formal) vs "alsjeblieft" (informal) for please.
Dutch prepositions are tricky – 'in/op/aan/bij' all translate to 'at' in different contexts.

conjugationExamples.tip: Diminutive -je: 'huis' → 'huisje'. After -s, just add -je.

topRepeated.tip: Swedish word order follows the V2 rule in main clauses.
Adverbs like "alltid" (always) and "aldrig" (never) go after the verb in main clauses.
Swedish uses definite suffixes: "-en"/"-et" for singular, "-na"/"-en" for plural.
Swedish verb groups: 1 (-ar), 2a (-er), 2b (-er), 3 (short, -r), 4 (irregular strong verbs).
"Hej" is informal, "God dag" is more formal.
When an adverb starts the sentence, subject and verb swap: "Idag åker jag" = Today I go.
Definite form adjectives add "-a": "den stora bilen" (the big car).
Swedish future uses "ska" (will/shall) or "kommer att" (going to).
Separable verbs split in main clauses: "Jag ringer upp dig" = I'll call you up.
Modal verbs: "kan" (can), "ska" (shall), "vill" (want), "måste" (must), "bör" (should).
